title: Stretch a $500 program budget with in-kind mapping
mechanism_check: A budget is not a pile of money, it is a pile of NEEDS. List every line item as a need, then ask which needs can be filled without cash.
In-kind goods (donated space, food, print) substitute for cash at ~the same face value — but only if someone actually asked for the item.
The mechanism is substitution: one cash line can vanish entirely if an in-kind source covers it; leftover cash concentrates where only cash works (permits, insurance, bus passes).
improvised_tools: A single-page 'needs board' (paper or shared doc): each need, its cash cost, and a blank column for the in-kind source
A standing ask script for donors: 'We need X; do you have one to lend or give?' — one ask per donor, not a generic plea
Receipt log for in-kind donations (date, donor, item, fair value) — auditors and grant reports require it
steps: List every program need for the event/season, with a cash price beside each. Total it.
Star the needs that legally or practically require cash (permits, insurance, fuel, gift cards). Everything else is in-kind-eligible.
Write the in-kind ask list: one sentence per need. Post it where donors see it (newsletter, lobby board, group chat).
Log each donation with date, donor, item, and fair value. Thank the donor the same day.
Re-run the budget with in-kind covered: cash now only pays starred lines. Reallocate surplus to the next program cycle, never to 'misc.'
stop_conditions: Stop if an in-kind 'donation' arrives with strings (branding you cannot honor, conditions you cannot meet) — decline politely; a poisoned gift costs more than cash.
Stop taking in-kind goods you cannot store or use within 30 days — they become a disposal bill.
Never promise a donor a tax deduction value yourself; refer them to their tax advisor and your finance lead.

title: Run a donation intake and sort with cardboard and volunteers
mechanism_check: Sorting is a conveyor, not a pile. Bottleneck is always triage speed, not donation volume.
Clothing/shoes/household arrive mixed; the mechanism is one-touch flow: every item is touched once, assigned to a lane, and never re-sorted.
Contamination (trash, broken, stained) must leave at intake, not downstream — one contaminated lane ruins the usable one beside it.
improvised_tools: Cardboard boxes or gaylords as lane bins, labeled with marker in 4-inch letters: KEEP / RAG-OUT / RECYCLE / CLIENT-PICK
A 6-foot folding table as the triage station — intake at one end, sorted bins at the other
Gloves, a sharps container (lidded bucket), and a 'question' bin for the supervisor's call
steps: Set lanes before the truck arrives: tables in a line, bins behind, intake volunteer at the door.
Intake volunteer does the fast triage: keep, rag-out, recycle. Nothing advances unless it is clean, intact, and usable.
Sorters work one lane each; when a bin is full they swap it for an empty and wheel the full one to staging — no stopping the line.
Sharps, liquids, batteries go straight to the supervisor bin. Do not sort them into lanes.
End of shift: count bins per lane, log poundage, and reconcile against the intake manifest.
stop_conditions: Stop the line immediately if you find syringes, bedbugs, or unknown chemicals — seal the box, isolate it, get the supervisor.
Stop accepting a category the moment its bins overflow with nowhere to stage — a flooded sort room is a fire-code violation, not generosity.
If volunteers cannot identify what an item is, it goes to the supervisor bin; never guess into a lane.

title: Produce a charity dinner event with borrowed gear
mechanism_check: An event is three machines running in parallel: front-of-house (guests feel welcome), program (the ask lands), and back-of-house (food/tables/bills get paid). Failure is almost always back-of-house because nobody staffs it.
Borrowed gear is free but unreliable — the mechanism is redundancy: every borrowed item needs a Plan B that fits in one car.
The ask is the product. Guests tolerate folding chairs; they do not tolerate a muddled ask with no number on the screen.
improvised_tools: A one-page run-of-show with minute-by-minute cues, printed in bulk — phones die, paper does not
Borrowed items list with owner names and return deadlines taped to each item
Two coolers as the emergency food/drink buffer; one 'fix box' (tape, zip ties, extension cords, first-aid, pens, change for the cash box)
steps: 60 days out: lock the ask (dollar goal, one named program), the room (donated venue), and the date. Everything else hangs off these.
Build the run-of-show backwards from the ask: doors, welcome, dinner, story, ask, thank-you, teardown. Assign a captain to each block.
Confirm every borrowed item twice: once at booking, once the week of. Replace anything unconfirmed with your Plan B.
Night-of: one captain runs the show from the printed sheet; the director works the room and makes the ask — never both jobs on one person.
Within 48 hours: thank donors, return borrowed gear on time, publish results against the goal. Return gear late once and it is gone next year.
stop_conditions: Stop adding program elements once the run-of-show exceeds what the room and crew can rehearse — every added skit is a minute stolen from the ask.
Cancel the ask segment's games/raffles if they require permits you do not hold — raffles without a license are illegal in most states.
If projected costs pass 30% of the fundraising goal, stop and redesign: you are running an expensive dinner, not a fundraiser.

title: Run event sound from a borrowed PA and one volunteer
mechanism_check: Sound failure is almost never the speakers — it is gain staging: mic too far from mouth, mixer gain too low, speaker gain too high. Feedback is a loop: mic hears speaker, speaker amplifies mic, repeat.
Speech needs intelligibility, not power: the mechanism is mic proximity. Every inch closer to the mouth is worth more than any knob.
Borrowed gear arrives with unknown history, so the test is load testing under real volume with a real talker, not a tap-tap.
improvised_tools: Borrowed PA head + speakers; a wired mic as primary (wireless as luxury, never the only mic)
A 50-foot extension cord and a power strip — venues never have an outlet where the PA wants to be
Gaffer tape for cable runs (not duct tape — it leaves residue and venues remember)
steps: Arrive two hours early. Place speakers in FRONT of the mics (toward the audience), never beside or behind them — that is the anti-feedback rule.
Set every channel: talk at normal volume into the mic from 4 inches away; bring channel gain up until it clips, then back off 20%.
Test with the actual MC reading the actual welcome at full room volume, doors closed. Walk every corner listening for dead spots.
Tape all cable runs flat across walking paths. Label the volume knob position with a marker dot so a volunteer cannot lose it.
Keep the wired mic as the backup in reach even if you run wireless. When a battery dies mid-speech, swap in under 10 seconds.
stop_conditions: Stop and cut power if the speakers smell hot or the mixer distorts at any gain — blown gear mid-event is worse than no gear.
Never run power and signal cables from the same venue breaker with the kitchen equipment — brownouts reboot mixers mid-program.
If feedback cannot be killed in three tries, mute the channel and hand the MC the wired mic closer to the mouth instead of chasing knobs.

title: Build a check-in desk from one phone and paper
mechanism_check: Check-in is a queue, and queues fail at one point: the lookup. Name search in a 400-row spreadsheet on a phone is the bottleneck.
The mechanism is pre-sorted lookup: alphabetical sections split the line across parallel workers. One worker, one alphabet slice.
Paper backup is not optional — if the phone dies at minute 5 of doors, the paper list IS the check-in.
improvised_tools: Printed attendee list, alphabetized, in large type — one copy per check-in worker
Wristbands or stickers for entry, meal, and VIP tiers — color does the credentialing so nobody memorizes names
A cash box with starting change and a single receipt pad if donations are taken at the door
steps: Before doors: split the list alphabetically (A–H, I–P, Q–Z) and post a sign over each station showing its slice.
Each worker: find name, hand band, mark the sheet. Three motions. If the name is not on the list, send them to the 'fix' table — never hold the line.
Fix table handles walk-ups, misspellings, and donor upgrades with a supervisor. The main line never stops for edge cases.
Count bands at the end and reconcile against marked names — the gap is your walk-up revenue audit.
stop_conditions: Stop adding check-in stations past the space the lobby allows — stations that block the fire exit get shut down by the venue mid-event.
If the list is lost and no paper backup exists, stop and rebuild from the email export on a laptop — do not work from memory; you will double-seat.
Never leave the cash box unattended, even for a minute. Two people touch the box at shift change, count aloud.

title: Run a food pantry line with one freezer and no waste
mechanism_check: A pantry line is inventory rotation under time pressure. The mechanism is FIFO plus temperature: perishables move first, and every minute at room temperature shortens shelf life.
Client choice (shopping model) wastes less than pre-bagged boxes, but only if the line keeps moving — a stalled line at the dairy case starves the intake.
Waste is the metric that kills funding: pounds distributed is the headline, pounds spoiled is the story you never want told.
improvised_tools: A whiteboard at intake showing today's stock per category — clients see limits before they choose, not at the register
Milk crates or banker boxes as client shopping carriers — one carrier per household keeps quantities fair without policing
A probe thermometer and a temperature log taped to the freezer — funders and health departments both ask for it
steps: Before clients arrive: stock shelves by expiry, soonest-expiring front and center. Log freezer temp.
Intake: verify eligibility per your policy, hand the carrier, point at the whiteboard limits.
Line flows one direction: dry goods, then refrigerated, then frozen last — frozen leaves the building still frozen.
Volunteer at each section restocks from the back and watches limits; one floater resolves disputes.
End of day: log pounds distributed by category, pull anything expired, clean and re-log the freezer temp.
stop_conditions: Stop distribution of any category the moment the freezer reads above safe temp for over two hours — log it, discard per food-safety rules, do not 'smell-test' your way out.
Stop the line if it backs out the door and blocks the parking lot — split into timed entry groups instead of one mob.
Never distribute recalled product; if a recall notice arrives mid-day, pull the item from every shelf immediately and log the pull.

title: Restore a donated laptop fleet for client use
mechanism_check: Donated machines arrive with unknown state: dead batteries, malware, personal data. The mechanism is wipe-first: nothing is trusted until the drive is wiped and the OS reinstalled clean.
The bottleneck is not hardware, it is uniformity: ten identical builds are maintainable; ten snowflakes are ten support tickets.
Battery is the lie detector — a laptop that dies in 20 minutes is a desktop with a handle, and clients plan around portability.
improvised_tools: USB boot sticks with a lightweight OS installer — one image for every machine
Compressed air, isopropyl alcohol, and a screwdriver set for cleaning and reseating RAM/storage
Asset tags and a spreadsheet: donor, serial, specs, build date, assigned client
steps: Intake: log donor, serial, and visible condition. Pull the drive and wipe it — no exceptions, no peeking at personal data (privacy is the law here).
Clean vents and fans, reseat RAM and storage, test the battery under load for 30 minutes.
Install the single standard image: OS, browser, office suite, and your organization's resource bookmarks. Nothing else.
Burn-in test: 24 hours of idle plus a video call test. Machines that fail go to parts, not to clients.
Tag the asset, record it, hand it out with a one-page care sheet and the return policy.
stop_conditions: Stop and quarantine any machine showing firmware-level tampering or that refuses a clean wipe — do not deploy it; recycle through a certified e-waste vendor.
Never hand out a machine with a client's predecessor's data still on it — that is a privacy breach with your organization's name on it.
If a machine needs a part that costs more than a refurbished replacement, stop restoring it and harvest it for parts.

title: Run an improvised fundraising booth at a street fair
mechanism_check: A street-fair booth competes with funnel cake. The mechanism is the 3-second hook: motion, color, and one sentence a passerby can read at walking speed.
Revenue comes from micro-transactions and sign-ups, not from long pitches — the booth that asks for $5 and an email beats the booth that explains the mission.
Foot traffic is tidal: setup before the surge, staff the surge at 2x, and tear down after the ebb. Staffing flat across the day wastes your volunteers.
improvised_tools: A 10x10 pop-up tent, a folding table, and a bold banner readable from 20 feet — borrowed or thrifted
A card reader on a charged phone plus a cash lockbox; a clipboard with a one-line email signup ('Get our story monthly')
A simple game or giveaway (spin wheel, guess-the-jar) as the stopping mechanism — people stop for play, then they hear the pitch
steps: Setup 90 minutes before gates: tent, banner, table at the FRONT edge (not buried at the back of the tent), game facing the walkway.
Staff in pairs: one runs the game and collects emails, one handles money and the 30-second pitch. Rotate every 90 minutes.
Every game player gets the one-sentence mission and the ask: '$5 feeds a family this week — can you skip one coffee?' Make the yes easy.
Log revenue hourly by type (cash, card, sign-ups). Photograph the booth for the funder report and socials.
Tear down in 30 minutes: cash counted by two people on the spot, gear returned the same day.
stop_conditions: Stop taking card payments the moment the reader loses signal and you cannot verify — switch to cash-only and sign-ups; never 'run it later' without a signed authorization.
If foot traffic dies (rain, competing main-stage act), stop staffing at 2x and collapse to one pair — protect volunteer energy for the next surge.
Never leave the booth unstaffed with the cash box out — one unstaffed minute is all it takes.

title: Print posters with zero print budget
mechanism_check: A poster works when it answers three questions in three seconds: what, when/where, and what do I do. Everything else is decoration.
The mechanism is contrast and hierarchy: one big headline, one date block, one call to action. If the headline cannot be read from across the street, the poster fails.
Distribution beats design: a perfect poster nobody sees is worth less than an ugly flyer in the right laundromat.
improvised_tools: A free design tool on a library computer (or phone) — one template reused for every event builds recognition
Black-and-white master copy: one good B&W print photocopied 50 times beats one color print seen by one person
A distribution map: the 20 spots in the neighborhood where your people actually look (laundromats, corner stores, bus stops, church boards)
steps: Write the poster backwards from the call to action: what do you want a stranger to DO? Put that in the biggest type after the headline.
Design once, in B&W: headline, date/time/place, one line on the mission, the action, contact. No paragraphs.
Print one master at the library; photocopy the stack. Cut a tear-off strip with the phone number at the bottom if handbills suit the venue.
Walk the distribution map in pairs; ask permission before posting on private boards. Photograph each posting for the file.
Pull expired posters after the event — leaving dead posters up trains the neighborhood to ignore yours.
stop_conditions: Stop designing after the second draft — poster perfectionism burns the distribution day, and distribution is the part that works.
Never post on utility poles, traffic signs, or other illegal surfaces; fines come out of the program budget you were trying to save.
If a venue says no, thank them and move on — arguing costs you the next venue that overhears.

title: Run programs in a borrowed space without owning a building
mechanism_check: Borrowed space is a relationship, not a room. The mechanism is being the guest who gets invited back: leave it cleaner, quieter, and more punctual than you found it.
The failure mode is setup/teardown time — programs that need 90 minutes of setup in a room you hold for 120 are underwater before the first client arrives.
Storage is the hidden constraint: if your supplies cannot live on one rolling cart, borrowed space will break you.
improvised_tools: A written use agreement, even one page: days, hours, setup/teardown windows, who locks up, insurance certificate on file
The 'go-bag cart': all program supplies on one rolling cart, inventoried with a photo so missing items are visible at a glance
A cleaning kit (broom, mop, trash bags, wipes) that travels with the cart — never rely on the host's supplies
steps: Negotiate the agreement around YOUR program's real needs: minimum 30 minutes setup and 30 teardown inside the window, locked storage if possible.
Run a timed dry-run of setup and teardown before the first session. If it does not fit the window, redesign the program, not the window.
Every session: arrive early, photograph the room on arrival, run the program, clean to the photo, lock up, text the host a thank-you.
Monthly: review the agreement with the host — usage counts, incidents, appreciation. Hosts who feel used end the arrangement.
stop_conditions: Stop using the space the moment insurance, background-check, or permit requirements lapse — an incident in an uninsured borrowed room can end the organization.
If setup consistently bleeds into program time for three sessions, stop and renegotiate the window or shrink the program — do not keep stealing from clients.
Never let a volunteer or client have unsupervised access to the host's other rooms or belongings; one incident ends the partnership and the program.

title: Combine a food drive, clothing drive, and sign-up into one event
mechanism_check: Three drives in one day share the only expensive resources: volunteers, space, and public attention. The mechanism is shared infrastructure with separated flows — one door in, three lanes, one door out.
The risk is cross-contamination of purpose: donors who brought food do not want a 10-minute enrollment pitch. The combine must stay opt-in at every lane.
Combined events multiply the story for funders: one event, three outcomes, one report — that is the leverage.
improvised_tools: The triage system from the donation-sort entry, scaled to three lanes with separate color-coded bins
One shared check-in (nonprofit-005 pattern) feeding three clearly signed lanes — one sentence each on what goes where
A single sign-up sheet per program with a 'text me info' option — paper plus a QR code to a form for the phone crowd
steps: Design the floor plan on paper first: one entrance, lanes side by side, one exit. Walk it yourself before volunteers arrive.
Staff each lane with a lane captain who owns only that lane; one floater roams with supplies and relief.
Every donor gets thanked once at exit, not pitched three times. Program sign-up is a visible opt-in table, not a gauntlet.
Track the three outcomes separately (pounds of food, bags of clothing, sign-ups) and report them as one event with three wins.
Debrief: which lane starved or flooded? Rebalance volunteers before the next combined event.
stop_conditions: Stop combining if one lane's line consistently blocks another's — the combine is hurting both; split them next time.
If any lane's quality standard collapses under volume (trash entering the food lane), pause intake for that lane until triage catches up.
Never merge the donor lists across programs without consent — sign-up for the newsletter is not consent for every mailing list.

title: Stand up emergency shelter overnight in your own office
mechanism_check: A call may come at 9 PM: a fire, a freeze, a family with nowhere to go. Call professional emergency services FIRST — your office is the bridge, not the destination.
The mechanism is minimum viable shelter: warmth, water, bathroom, a safe place to sleep, and a plan for morning. Everything else is tomorrow's problem.
Safety scales down fast at 2 AM: fewer staff, tired volunteers, unfamiliar clients. Two-deep staffing is non-negotiable — never one adult alone with clients.
improvised_tools: A go-bag for the building: blankets, bottled water, phone chargers, a lockable cash/doc box, flashlights, cleaning supplies
A laminated one-page emergency protocol posted by the door: who calls whom, in what order
A contact sheet: local shelter hotline, Red Cross chapter, police non-emergency, on-call board member — printed, not just in a phone
steps: Call 911 / emergency services FIRST if anyone is in danger, injured, or the building is unsafe. Your shelter role starts after professionals are engaged.
Assess the space: lock everything that should stay locked (offices, kitchens with gas, supply rooms). One public area only.
Set up sleeping: blankets spaced out, bathroom access clear and lit, one volunteer awake on watch at all times.
Log every person: name, contact, needs, medications, children. This log protects them and you.
At first light: hand off to the professional shelter system or caseworker. Your office returns to office by end of day.
stop_conditions: Call emergency services first — this entry's first stop is professionals, not improvisation. Do not attempt medical care beyond basic first aid.
Do NOT attempt this if the building is unsafe (fire damage, no heat in a freeze, no working locks) — relocate to the professional shelter instead.
Stop and evacuate to the professional system if anyone becomes violent, intoxicated beyond control, or a child-protection issue arises — call 911 and the on-call supervisor.
Never house unaccompanied minors without the supervisor and child-welfare protocol engaged; that is a legal boundary, not a judgment call.

title: Restore a donor database from a messy spreadsheet
mechanism_check: A messy spreadsheet is still data — the mechanism is normalize before you migrate: one row per gift, one column per fact, no merged cells, no color-coding as data.
Duplicates are the cancer: the same donor spelled three ways splits their giving history and makes your top-donor list a lie.
Every cleanup step must be reversible: work on a copy, keep the original frozen. One bad find-and-replace without a backup is unrecoverable.
improvised_tools: A frozen copy of the original file, dated, stored separately — the 'do not touch' archive
A dedupe pass using email + phone as the match key (names lie; contact points do not)
A simple data dictionary: what each column means, written down once, so the next person does not re-invent it
steps: Freeze and copy the original. Every cleanup happens on the working copy only.
Standardize columns: First, Last, Email, Phone, Address, GiftDate, GiftAmount, Campaign, Notes. Split combined cells apart.
Dedupe: sort by email, merge duplicates keeping the most complete record; log every merge (which rows combined, when, by whom).
Validate: spot-check 20 random donors against source records (receipts, bank deposits). If more than 2 are wrong, your process is broken — fix the process, not the rows.
Write the data dictionary and the entry rules; future messes get prevented at the door, not cleaned after.
stop_conditions: Stop and restore from the frozen copy if a bulk operation corrupts the working file — redo the step slower; do not hand-edit 2,000 rows.

If the spreadsheet contains donor financial data (card numbers, bank accounts), stop immediately and escalate to the treasurer — that data should never have been in a spreadsheet, and cleanup now includes a security review.
Never delete the original until the restored database has run one full reporting cycle (thank-yous, one appeal, one report) without error.

title: Build a volunteer driver network for client transport
mechanism_check: Transport is the invisible barrier: clients miss appointments, jobs, and court dates for lack of a ride. The mechanism is scheduled redundancy — every critical ride has a primary and a backup driver confirmed the night before.
Volunteer drivers donate time but absorb risk: insurance, background checks, and vehicle standards are the price of admission, not paperwork to skip.
The dispatch problem is matching: right driver, right car (car seat? wheelchair?), right time, right client. One shared sheet beats ten text threads.
improvised_tools: A driver packet: application, background-check consent, insurance verification, vehicle checklist — completed before the first ride
A shared dispatch sheet: date, client (first name + code, never full details in a shared doc), pickup, destination, driver, backup, status
A mileage log for reimbursement or tax documentation — drivers who pay for gas quit; reimbursed drivers stay
steps: Recruit drivers with the honest pitch: set routes, set shifts, real impact. Screen every driver before they drive anyone.
Build the dispatch sheet and a simple request flow: staff submit ride requests 48 hours out; dispatcher assigns by the night before.
Confirm every ride twice: assignment confirmation, then a day-of text to driver and client. No confirmation, no ride — the backup activates.
Log every completed ride with mileage. Reimburse monthly, on time — late reimbursement is the fastest way to lose drivers.
Quarterly: review incidents, no-shows, and driver feedback. Retire the sheet and upgrade to scheduling software only when the sheet breaks.
stop_conditions: Stop a driver immediately after any at-fault incident, DUI, or lapsed insurance — no second chances on client safety; re-screening is mandatory.
Do not transport unaccompanied minors without the two-deep rule and written guardian consent on file — that is the legal floor.
If ride requests consistently exceed driver capacity, stop over-promising and cap the schedule — a missed critical ride (court, chemo) destroys trust faster than a waitlist does.

title: Read a nonprofit 990 and financial statement like staff
mechanism_check: A 990 is a nonprofit's public tax return — revenue, expenses, executive pay, and program-vs-overhead ratios, all public by law.

The mechanism is ratio reading: program expense ratio (mission spending / total spending) and fundraising efficiency (fundraising cost / funds raised) tell you health at a glance; the narrative tells you whether the numbers are honest.
Career leverage: staff who can read the 990 ask better questions in interviews, write better grants, and spot a sinking employer before signing on.
improvised_tools: The organization's last three 990s (free on public nonprofit databases) — trend beats snapshot
A highlighter and a one-page ratio worksheet: program ratio, admin ratio, fundraising efficiency, months of cash on hand
The audited financial statements if available — the 990 is the summary, the audit is the receipts
steps: Pull three years of 990s. Compute the program expense ratio for each year; watch the trend, not one year's number.
Read Part IX (expenses) line by line: which costs grew, which shrank, and does the story in the mission statement match where money went?
Check officer compensation (Part VII) against the budget size — a $60k org paying a $120k director is a red flag; a $5M org paying $90k is a different story.
Read the balance sheet: months of cash on hand = cash / (annual expenses / 12). Under 3 months means fragile; over 12 means hoarding or saving for something — ask which.
Bring one question the numbers raised to your next team meeting. Reading without asking changes nothing.
stop_conditions: Stop drawing conclusions from a single year — one bad year is weather; three years is climate.
Do not accuse or gossip based on 990 findings; ask questions privately to finance staff first — public data still deserves private handling.
If the org has no 990 on file and no audit and will not explain why, stop trusting its financial story until it does.

title: Write a grant budget that matches the narrative
mechanism_check: Grant reviewers read budget and narrative side by side, hunting for lies: a narrative promising weekly home visits with a budget showing no mileage line gets rejected on page two.
The mechanism is line-by-line mirroring: every activity the narrative promises appears as a costed line; every costed line appears in the narrative.
Funders fund outcomes through activities through costs — the budget is the narrative translated into dollars, not a separate document.
improvised_tools: The funder's budget template and its allowed/disallowed cost list — read this BEFORE writing a word of narrative
Your org's chart of accounts and current indirect rate (or the de minimis 10% if you have no negotiated rate)
Last year's actuals for the same program — real costs beat estimates, and reviewers can tell
steps: Read the funder's guidelines twice: allowable costs, match requirements, indirect cap, budget period. Build a checklist of their rules.
Draft the narrative's activity list first, then cost each activity: personnel (with % time), fringe, supplies, travel, contracts, other direct.
Mirror-check: walk the narrative paragraph by paragraph and point at the budget line that pays for each promised activity. Fill every gap.
Add the indirect line per the funder's cap; never hide admin costs inside program lines — reviewers spot it and trust evaporates.
Have someone who did NOT write it do the mirror-check again cold. Fix, then submit with the narrative attached as one story.
stop_conditions: Stop if the funder's requirements would force you to misrepresent costs (hiding admin, inventing match) — decline the grant; a won-by-lying grant is an audit time bomb.
If the budget cannot cover the promised activities at real cost, stop and shrink the promise — never submit a budget you know is fiction.
Never submit past the deadline hoping for grace; late is rejected unread at most foundations.

title: Assemble a first grant application from a boilerplate kit
mechanism_check: A first application fails on completeness, not brilliance: missing attachments kill more applications than weak prose.
The mechanism is the boilerplate kit — mission, history, program descriptions, bios, budget template — maintained once, reused forever, customized per funder.
Funders ask the same 12 questions in different order. Answer them once well and you have answered 80% of every future application.
improvised_tools: A boilerplate folder: 1-page mission/history, program one-pagers, board list, staff bios, last audit/990, IRS determination letter, budget template
The funder's application checklist, printed and taped to the wall — every item gets a checkmark and a filename
A calendar with the deadline minus 14 days (internal draft deadline) and minus 7 days (final review)
steps: Read the funder's guidelines and build their exact checklist: narrative limits, required attachments, budget format, submission portal quirks.
Pull each answer from the boilerplate kit; customize only what the funder specifically asks about (their priorities, their geography, their outcomes).
Write the need statement with local data (your county, your waitlist) — generic national statistics signal a generic application.
Assemble the full package 7 days early: narrative, budget (mirrored per nonprofit-016), attachments, signatures. Review it cold once.
Submit, then log everything: funder, amount, deadline, decision date, contact. The log is next year's head start.
stop_conditions: Stop customizing boilerplate into fiction — if the kit does not truthfully answer a question, write a new true answer; never stretch one.
If required attachments (audit, determination letter) are missing or expired, stop and fix those first — the application is dead without them.
Never let one person write, review, and submit alone; the solo pipeline is where wrong-file uploads and missed deadlines hide.

title: Run a donor stewardship cadence: thank in 48 hours
mechanism_check: Donor retention is cheaper than acquisition by an order of magnitude, and the mechanism is speed plus specificity: a fast, specific thank-you outperforms a slow, generic one every time.
The 48-hour rule: a donor thanked within two days gives again at dramatically higher rates. After a week, the gift is emotionally forgotten.
Stewardship is a cadence, not an event: thank, report impact, thank again, then ask. Asking before reporting is the sequence that burns lists.
improvised_tools: A thank-you template with three blanks: amount, program, one concrete outcome ('your $50 stocked the pantry shelf Tuesday')
A 48-hour tickler: every gift logged same-day, thank-you out within two business days — phone call for major gifts, letter/email for the rest
An impact-report calendar: quarterly one-page updates showing what donor money did, sent BEFORE the next appeal
steps: Log every gift the day it arrives: donor, amount, date, designation, source. No gift sits unlogged overnight.
Send the thank-you within 48 hours: specific amount, specific program, specific outcome. Sign it by a human, not the org.
File the donor's preference (email/mail/phone, interests) at the same time — the next touch uses what they told you.
Quarterly: send the impact update to every donor before any new appeal goes out. Then, and only then, make the next ask.
Track retention rate (donors who gave last year and this year). If it drops two quarters running, the cadence is broken — audit the 48-hour rule first.
stop_conditions: Stop sending appeals to donors who have asked to be removed or to hear less — every unwanted appeal is a lost donor and, in some channels, a legal problem.
If a major donor's gift arrives with restrictions you cannot honor, stop and call them before depositing — returning a misused restricted gift is far worse than a hard conversation.
Never fabricate impact numbers for the update; one caught exaggeration ends more donor relationships than any silence.

title: Turn one program story into a donor appeal letter
mechanism_check: Donors give to people, not programs. The mechanism is the single-protagonist story: one client, one arc, one outcome — statistics support the story, never lead it.
The arc is before → intervention → after, in the client's own dignity: the story must leave the client looking strong, not pitiful. Pity raises money once and costs you the community's trust.
The ask must be concrete and priced: '$50 does X' converts; 'please support our mission' does not.
improvised_tools: One true client story with written consent to share it (signed release on file — non-negotiable)
The program's real unit costs: what $25, $50, $250 actually buy — priced from the budget, not invented
A photo with consent, or a dignified illustration if the client prefers anonymity
steps: Interview for the arc: what was life like before, what did the program do specifically, what changed. Record exact quotes — quotes carry the letter.
Get the signed story release BEFORE writing a word. No release, no story, no exceptions.
Draft the letter: open on the person (not the org), one paragraph of before, the intervention in plain words, the after with one real number.
Place the priced ask after the story: three giving levels tied to real outcomes, plus a reply device (envelope, link, QR).
Read it back asking: would the client be proud to read this aloud? If not, rewrite until yes. Then mail and track response rate.
stop_conditions: Stop and kill the story if consent is withdrawn at any point — published or not, the client's 'no' is final and immediate.
Never invent or composite details ('a typical client'); one discovered fabrication destroys the appeal and the org's credibility.
Do not use a client's full name, photo, or identifying details without explicit written consent covering exactly that use.

title: Run a board meeting that ends on time with decisions
mechanism_check: Board meetings fail by agenda bloat: 90 minutes of reports, 10 minutes of decisions, and the real choices get punted.
The mechanism is consent agenda + decision-first ordering: routine items approved in one vote, decisions up front while minds are fresh, reports last and short.
A board that does not decide is a board that does not govern — and an ED without board decisions is exposed on every hard call.
improvised_tools: A timed agenda sent 5 days prior: decision items first with background memos attached, consent agenda second, reports last
A one-page dashboard: cash on hand, program numbers vs. target, fundraising vs. goal — the same three numbers every meeting
A parking lot list and a decisions log: what was decided, who owns it, by when — read back before adjournment
steps: Send the packet 5 days out: agenda, dashboard, memos for each decision item, last meeting's decisions log with status.
Open on time with the decisions: each gets its memo, a motion, discussion, vote. Time-box discussion (10 min default, extendable once).
Consent agenda: one vote approves minutes, routine financials, committee reports — anything needing discussion gets pulled out individually.
Reports last, 5 minutes each, exceptions only: 'on track' needs no speech. End with the decisions log read-back.
Within 48 hours: send minutes with the decisions log. Owners get their deadlines in writing.
stop_conditions: Stop the meeting from becoming a staff work session — if the board is designing the program, governance has failed; send it back to committee.
If quorum is lost mid-meeting, stop taking binding votes; record discussion and ratify next time — decisions without quorum are void.
Never let one member filibuster a decision past the time-box twice; the chair moves to vote — politeness that prevents decisions is not kindness.

title: Build a monthly-donor pipeline from zero
mechanism_check: Monthly donors are the highest-value segment: retention 2-3x annual donors, and predictable revenue lets you plan instead of panic.
The mechanism is friction removal: the ask is small ($10–25/month), the signup is one page, and the upgrade path (annual → monthly) is offered at every touchpoint.
Acquisition is the expensive part; the pipeline pays for itself in month 4–6. Anyone judging it on month 1 will kill it.
improvised_tools: A donation page with monthly pre-selected (not hidden behind a toggle) and three suggested amounts tied to outcomes
An upgrade script for existing annual donors: 'Your $120 a year becomes $10 a month — same gift, steadier impact'
A monthly-donor welcome series: immediate thank-you, day-7 impact story, day-30 'you're part of the crew' — then the regular cadence
steps: Set the foundation: monthly option live, tested on phone, one-page signup. If signup takes more than 2 minutes, fix it before promoting.
Launch to warm audiences first: current donors (upgrade ask), volunteers, event attendees. Cold acquisition comes after the funnel works.
Run the welcome series for every new monthly donor automatically — the first 30 days decide whether month 2 happens.
Report to monthly donors as a cohort: '412 sustainers kept the pantry open every Tuesday this quarter.' Belonging retains.
Track: conversion rate, month-2 retention, 12-month value vs. acquisition cost. Scale what the numbers bless; kill what they don't.
stop_conditions: Stop promoting the monthly program if the signup page fails on mobile — most donors arrive on phones; a broken mobile form burns the audience.
If month-2 retention drops below half, stop acquiring and fix the welcome series first — pouring donors into a leaking bucket wastes the acquisition spend.
Never switch a donor to monthly without explicit consent, and make cancellation one click — dark patterns on donations are unethical and, in some places, illegal.

title: Negotiate an in-kind corporate sponsorship
mechanism_check: Companies prefer giving product over cash: it costs them wholesale, values at retail, and photographs well. The mechanism is making the ask specific, easy, and visible.
The negotiation is a trade, not a beg: you offer audience, goodwill, and a tax receipt; they offer goods. Both sides should be able to state what they get in one sentence.
In-kind sponsorships die in vagueness: 'support our event' gets ignored; 'donate 200 hot dogs for 300 guests on June 4, logo on the banner' gets a yes.
improvised_tools: A one-page sponsorship menu: 3 tiers with exact deliverables on both sides (what they give, what they get, logo placement, audience size)
The in-kind needs list from the budget exercise (nonprofit-001) — the ask list IS the negotiation inventory
A fulfillment checklist per sponsor: logo received, banner printed, thank-you sent, receipt issued — sponsors who feel forgotten never return
steps: Target companies whose product matches your need (food vendor for the dinner, printer for the posters) — relevance beats size.
Make the ask in writing with the tier menu attached: specific item, specific quantity, specific date, specific recognition.
Negotiate the recognition honestly: promise only the audience you actually have. Inflated attendance numbers are discovered and remembered.
Confirm in writing: what, how many, delivery date and place, who unloads. Verbal sponsorships evaporate.
Deliver every promised recognition, send the tax receipt and a photo of their product in action within a week. Then ask about next year.
stop_conditions: Stop pursuing a sponsor that demands recognition you cannot deliver (naming rights you do not own, endorsements you cannot make) — walk away politely.
If a sponsor's product or practices conflict with your mission, decline the gift — mission-incompatible money costs more in trust than it pays in goods.
Never promise exclusivity you cannot enforce ('only your brand at the event') unless you control every vendor and donor table.

title: Combine program metrics into one funder report
mechanism_check: Funders drown in reports; the one they remember leads with outcomes, not activities. The mechanism is the logic model: inputs → activities → outputs → outcomes, one page, numbers attached.
Combining metrics across programs works only if the definitions match: 'served' must mean the same thing in every program, or the total is fiction.
The report is a retention tool: a funder who can quote your outcomes to their board renews. Write the sentences you want them to quote.
improvised_tools: A shared definitions sheet: what counts as 'served', 'completed', 'placed' — agreed once, used everywhere
The logic model one-pager per program, then one combined page: totals plus the two or three outcomes that matter most
Two client stories with releases (nonprofit-019 pattern) — the numbers prove scale, the stories prove humanity
steps: Lock definitions first: align every program's counting rules before the reporting period starts, not during.
Collect monthly, not annually: a simple sheet per program, same format, due the 5th. Annual reconstruction from memory is fiction.
Draft the combined report: one page of outcomes with totals, one page per program detail, stories woven in, budget-vs-actual attached.
Have program staff verify their numbers before it goes out — the person who ran the program must recognize the report.
Send on time, then log it: funder, period, due date, sent date. Late reports are the #1 reason renewals stall.
stop_conditions: Stop and fix definitions if two programs count the same client twice and you cannot un-duplicate — report the overlap honestly rather than inflating totals.
If the numbers show a program missing its targets, report it with the corrective plan — hiding bad numbers is discovered eventually and believed never again.
Never copy last year's narrative with new numbers; funders compare, and a stale narrative signals a stale program.

title: Level a nonprofit career: volunteer to program coordinator
mechanism_check: Nonprofit hiring runs on demonstrated competence, not credentials: the person who already runs the pantry shift gets the coordinator title before the outsider with the degree.
The mechanism is the paper trail: every responsibility you absorb gets documented (hours, outcomes, people supervised) until your resume writes itself.
Titles lag reality by 6–12 months in small orgs. The career move is to do the coordinator work, document it, then ask for the title and pay to match — in that order.
improvised_tools: A running 'brag file': every project, the numbers, the people, the dates — updated monthly, not reconstructed at job-hunt time
One skill gap closed per quarter: grant basics, supervision, data, public speaking — the four that unlock coordinator pay bands
A mentor inside the sector: one working coordinator who will review your resume and tell you the truth about openings
steps: Map the coordinator job descriptions in your area: list the required skills, mark which you have demonstrated, which are gaps.
Volunteer strategically for the gaps: offer to run the volunteer shift (supervision), own the monthly numbers (data), draft the next small grant (writing).
Document everything into the brag file as it happens: 'Supervised 12 volunteers across 40 pantry shifts; cut client wait time 25%.'
Translate the brag file into a resume in the sector's language: outcomes first, mission second, duties last.
Ask for the promotion with the file in hand, or take the file to the next org. Loyalty without documentation is just tenure.
stop_conditions: Stop doing coordinator-level work indefinitely without the title or pay conversation — after 6 months of documented performance, ask; after 12 with no movement, take the file elsewhere.
Do not pad the brag file: one verifiable lie discovered in a reference check ends a nonprofit career in a small community.
If the org cannot pay coordinator wages, negotiate the title plus a raise timeline in writing — a title without a plan is a stall.

title: Write a 30-second elevator pitch for the mission
mechanism_check: Nobody remembers mission statements; they remember one vivid sentence. The mechanism is problem → action → proof, in 30 seconds, in plain words.
The pitch fails two ways: jargon ('we leverage synergistic stakeholder paradigms') and abstraction ('we empower communities'). Both are forgettable.
One pitch, three endings: the donor ending (the ask), the volunteer ending (the invitation), the partner ending (the collaboration). Same core, different last line.
improvised_tools: Three index cards: the 30-second core, and one line each for the donor/volunteer/partner endings
One real number (people served, meals, nights of shelter) and one real name-with-consent (or 'a mom of three') for the proof line
A mirror or a patient friend — the pitch is spoken, so it must be rehearsed out loud, not just written
steps: Draft the core: 'Every [time period], [number] of [people] in [place] face [problem]. We [concrete action]. Last year [proof].' Fill the brackets with real words.
Cut every adjective and every piece of jargon. Read it aloud; if you stumble, the sentence is wrong, not you.
Add the ending for the audience in front of you: donor ('$50 stocks the shelf Tuesday'), volunteer ('we need Saturday hands'), partner ('we need your kitchen Thursdays').
Rehearse until it sounds like talking, not reciting. Time it: 25–35 seconds.
Use it everywhere for a month and note which ending gets responses; keep the winners, rewrite the losers.
stop_conditions: Stop at 30 seconds — a 90-second 'elevator pitch' is a speech, and speeches end conversations instead of starting them.
Never pitch without the proof line; a pitch with no number and no story is just a slogan.
If the listener's eyes glaze, stop pitching and ask a question — the pitch opens the door, curiosity walks through it.

title: Debrief a declined grant and reapply stronger
mechanism_check: Most rejections are not verdicts on the mission — they are fit, timing, or competition. The mechanism is the debrief: extract the real reason before the disappointment hardens into a story.
Funders who decline often give feedback if asked within two weeks, politely, once. That feedback is worth more than the application effort.
Reapplication is a separate skill from application: same funder, new cycle, visibly stronger — reviewers remember improvement.
improvised_tools: The decline letter and the original application side by side — read the letter for what it actually says, not what it feels like
A debrief template: what we claimed, what they fund, where the gap was, what changes before reapplying
A relationship log: program officer name, feedback received, next cycle date — decline is the start of the relationship, not the end
steps: Within 48 hours: log the decline, notify the team, park the disappointment. No rewriting while stinging.
Within two weeks: call or email the program officer once — thank them, ask for 15 minutes of feedback on fit and competitiveness. Accept whatever they give.
Debrief honestly: was it fit (wrong funder), strength (right funder, weak app), or timing (right app, brutal cycle)? Different causes, different fixes.
Fix the real cause: rewrite the weak section, gather the missing data, or redirect to a better-fit funder. Do not resubmit the same application.
Reapply next cycle visibly improved, referencing the feedback ('per your guidance, we now track X'). Funders fund learners.
stop_conditions: Stop reapplying to the same funder with the same application — three identical submissions marks you as uncoachable.
If feedback reveals a fundamental mission mismatch, stop pursuing that funder entirely; redirect the effort to fit.
Never badmouth the funder to peers or on social media — the sector is small, program officers talk, and the next application dies on arrival.

title: Train a volunteer crew in 30 minutes flat
mechanism_check: Volunteers arrive willing but unskilled, and their attention expires in about 30 minutes. The mechanism is show-one-do-one: demonstrate the task once, have them do it once supervised, then release.
Training fails when it is a lecture. Volunteers learn the pantry line by running the pantry line, not by hearing about it.
The real product of training is not skill, it is confidence: a volunteer who has done the task once will return; one who only watched will not.
improvised_tools: A one-page role card per station: 3 bullet task list, who to ask, where the bathroom is — laminated if possible
A buddy system: every new volunteer paired with a returning one for the first shift
The 30-minute clock: 5 min welcome + mission, 10 min demo, 10 min supervised practice, 5 min questions and assignment
steps: Welcome (5 min): the mission in one sentence, today's goal in one number, where things are. No org history lecture.
Demo (10 min): show the single most common task start to finish, narrating the why, not just the what.
Practice (10 min): each volunteer does the task once while the buddy watches. Correct gently, praise specifically.
Assign (5 min): hand out role cards, pair buddies, state the shift end time and the thank-you at the end.
Close the loop: thank the crew by name at shift end, note who excelled for future captain roles.
stop_conditions: Stop training when the 30 minutes are up — a 60-minute orientation for a 2-hour shift loses more volunteers than it prepares.
Never assign a volunteer to client-facing or safety-critical work they have not practiced once supervised.
If a volunteer clearly cannot do the task safely after practice, reassign them kindly to a fitting role — do not hope it works out.

title: Hold the two-deep rule: never solo a client contact
mechanism_check: One staff member alone with a client is a risk to both: the client has no witness if something goes wrong, and the staffer has no defense against a false claim.
The mechanism is structural, not trust-based: the schedule itself requires two adults present for every client interaction — no exceptions, no 'just this once.'
Two-deep also protects against burnout: solo crisis work is the fastest path to a staffer quitting, and shared shifts share the weight.
improvised_tools: A scheduling rule written into policy: every shift, visit, and transport has two named adults — the shift is not staffed until both are confirmed
A check-in/check-out log: who is with which client, where, and when they return — visible to the supervisor on duty
A panic word and a phone tree: any staffer can call for backup without explaining why first
steps: Write the rule into the volunteer handbook and staff policy: two adults, line of sight or earshot, every client contact.
Build every schedule with pairs, not individuals: if only one adult is available, the activity is rescheduled, not run solo.
Log every client contact: pair names, location, time in/out. The log is reviewed weekly, not filed away.
Brief every new hire and volunteer on day one: the rule, the why, and the panic word. Test that they know it.
Audit quarterly: pull two weeks of logs and verify compliance. Gaps get fixed in the schedule, not with a memo.
stop_conditions: Stop any activity immediately if the second adult leaves — the remaining staffer ends the contact and regroups; the program waits.
Never waive the rule for 'trusted' staff or 'easy' clients — the rule protects precisely the situations that feel safe.
If staffing cannot sustain two-deep for a program, suspend the program until it can — running it solo is not an option.

title: Run a shift handoff logbook that survives chaos
mechanism_check: Information dies between shifts: the morning crew never hears what the night crew saw. The mechanism is the written handoff — three lines per shift, read before starting.
The log works because it is ritual, not optional: outgoing writes it, incoming reads it aloud, both sign. Rituals survive chaos; good intentions do not.
The three lines are: what happened, what is pending, what to watch. Anything longer goes in the incident report; the log stays scannable.
improvised_tools: A bound logbook (not loose paper) at the handoff station, with the three-line template printed inside the cover
A 5-minute overlap built into the schedule — handoff without overlap is a note left on a desk, not a handoff
A red-flag convention: anything safety-related gets a red star in the margin and a verbal call-out, not just ink
steps: Outgoing shift writes before leaving: what happened (facts), what is pending (who owes what), what to watch (people, equipment, moods).
Incoming shift reads the last entry aloud at overlap; outgoing answers questions. Both initial the entry.
Red-star items get a verbal briefing plus a supervisor notification — the log records it, the voice ensures it lands.
Supervisor reviews the log weekly: patterns (recurring incidents, repeated pendings) become agenda items, not surprises.
Monthly: one page summarizing the log's patterns goes to leadership. The log is data, not just memory.
stop_conditions: Stop and escalate immediately if a handoff reveals an unreported safety incident — backfill the incident report before the next shift starts.
If the log goes three shifts without entries, the ritual is dead — stop and rebuild it with the crew rather than letting a blank book pretend.
Never use the logbook for personnel complaints or gossip; it is an operational record and may be read in audits or legal review.

title: Improvise roles when half the crew no-shows
mechanism_check: No-shows are normal in volunteer crews: plan for 70% attendance, celebrate 100%. The mechanism is role compression — merge roles by priority, cut by priority, never stretch everyone thin.
The failure mode is heroic coverage: four people doing eight jobs badly. Compressed roles done well beat full roles done dangerously.
Triage the program, not the people: rank every function as must-happen, should-happen, or cuttable — then staff the musts first.
improvised_tools: A priority-ranked role list made BEFORE the event: must / should / cuttable, with each role's minimum staffing
Cross-trained floaters: two volunteers trained on two stations each, held in reserve for exactly this moment
A pre-written 'thin crew' script: which stations merge, which close, announced confidently so clients never feel the chaos
steps: Count actual crew 60 minutes before start. If below 80% of plan, activate thin-crew mode — decide early, not mid-event.
Compress by the priority list: merge should-roles into must-roles, close cuttable stations with a polite sign.
Re-brief the crew on their compressed roles: one sentence each — 'You own intake AND the fix table now.'
Run the handoff log (nonprofit-029) with extra care: thin crews forget more, so write more down.
After: thank the crew double, log who no-showed without notice, and adjust next event's confirmation process.
stop_conditions: Stop and cancel rather than run if must-happen roles cannot be staffed safely — an unsafe event is worse than a cancelled one.
Never compress the two-deep rule (nonprofit-028) or safety roles into one person — those merge with nothing.
If no-shows are chronic from the same volunteers, stop scheduling them for critical roles; reliability is a qualification.

title: De-escalate an agitated client or volunteer
mechanism_check: If anyone is in danger, call 911 FIRST — de-escalation is for agitation, not for violence in progress.
Agitation is a nervous system event, not a character flaw. The mechanism is lowering stimulation: your calm voice, open posture, and fewer words reduce their arousal; arguing raises it.
The goal is not to win or to fix — it is to return the person to a state where they can think. Everything else waits.
improvised_tools: A calm room or corner: low traffic, an exit the person can see (never block their path out), chairs at an angle not face-to-face
The two-deep rule in effect: one person talks, the second stays nearby as witness and backup — never de-escalate alone
A de-escalation script card: listen, reflect, offer choices, set the boundary — carried, not memorized under stress
steps: Ensure safety first: position yourself near the exit, keep the second staffer in sight, remove onlookers kindly.
Listen without interrupting for 60 seconds. Then reflect back what you heard: 'It sounds like you're upset because...' — being heard lowers arousal.
Offer two acceptable choices: 'We can talk here or step outside — which works?' Choice restores a sense of control.
State the boundary once, calmly: 'I want to help, and I need you to lower your voice so we can.' Then wait.
If they de-escalate: solve the solvable part now, schedule the rest. Document the incident factually within the hour.
stop_conditions: Call 911 first if there is any threat of violence, a weapon, or someone is being harmed — do not attempt de-escalation on violence in progress.
Do NOT attempt this alone, do not touch an agitated person, and do not block their exit — any of these can turn agitation into assault.
Stop engaging and disengage if de-escalation fails after two calm attempts — withdraw, keep distance, call for help. Persistence becomes provocation.
Never promise outcomes you cannot deliver to calm someone down; the lie detonates later and destroys trust permanently.

title: Run the burnout watch: the three-signal check
mechanism_check: Burnout in nonprofit staff is not a personal failing — it is an organizational output. The mechanism is early detection: three observable signals, checked monthly, trigger support before collapse.

The three signals: cynicism (contempt for clients or mission), exhaustion (tired after rest), and inefficacy (work that used to matter feels pointless). One signal is a bad week; two sustained is the watch; three is the alarm.
The fix is structural (load, control, recognition), not a pizza party. Wellness initiatives that do not change workload are decoration.
improvised_tools: A monthly 10-minute check-in ritual: supervisor asks the three signals directly, in private, with no performance judgment attached
A load board: every staffer's active projects visible in one place — invisible overload is the norm, visible overload is fixable
A relief bench: cross-trained backup for every critical role so time off is actually possible (see nonprofit-035)
steps: Monthly, in the 1:1: ask the three signals plainly. Listen. Record only the support plan, not a diagnosis.
At two sustained signals: act on load first — what can pause, delegate, or drop this month? Name it specifically.
Restore control: let the staffer choose what to shed and what the recovery looks like (schedule change, project pause, real time off).
Recognize specifically: name the actual work they did and its actual effect. Generic praise does not touch inefficacy.
Quarterly, review the load board as a team: redistribute before the next quarter, not after someone breaks.
stop_conditions: Stop treating burnout as a resilience problem — if multiple staff hit the alarm, the workload or structure is the problem, not the people.
If a staffer shows signs of clinical depression or anxiety, stop at support and refer to professional help — supervisors coach workload, not mental health.
Never punish honesty in the check-in: one staffer penalized for admitting exhaustion ends the ritual for everyone, permanently.

title: Run a 10-minute daily standup for field staff
mechanism_check: Field staff scatter across sites and lose sync by noon. The mechanism is the 10-minute alignment: same time, same three questions, standing up (literally) so nobody settles in.
The three questions: what did you finish, what are you doing today, what is blocking you. Blockers are the product — everything else is status.
Standups die two deaths: they become 30-minute meetings, or they become rituals nobody needs. The timer and the parking lot prevent both.
improvised_tools: A visible timer (phone is fine) and a hard 10-minute stop — the constraint is the feature
A parking lot list: any topic needing more than 30 seconds goes there for after, not into the standup
A shared blocker board: blockers named in standup get an owner and a due time before the crew disperses
steps: Same time every day, before field deployment. Everyone stands. Timer starts.
Round-robin, 60 seconds each: done, doing, blocked. No problem-solving during shares — blockers get named, not solved.
After the round: assign each blocker an owner and a check-in time. Parking-lot items get 5 minutes max or a separate meeting.
Timer ends it at 10 minutes, solved or not. Unfinished business goes to the blocker board, not into overtime.
Weekly: review the blocker board for patterns — the same blocker three days running is a system problem, not a personal one.
stop_conditions: Stop holding the standup if the team is under 3 people or fully co-located doing one task — the ritual must earn its 10 minutes or be cut.
If one person dominates past their 60 seconds twice, the facilitator cuts them off kindly — the standup belongs to the crew, not the loudest.
Never use standup for performance criticism; blockers are system failures to fix, not people to blame — blame ends honesty.

title: Resolve staff-versus-volunteer friction fast
mechanism_check: Staff-volunteer friction is structural: staff carry accountability, volunteers carry freedom, and each resents the other's position. The mechanism is naming the structural cause before addressing the personal clash.
Friction festers because nobody owns it: staff think the volunteer coordinator handles it, the coordinator thinks the supervisor does. The rule is: whoever sees it first, surfaces it within 48 hours.
Resolution is fast or it is not resolution — a conflict left for a month becomes a faction, and factions end volunteer programs.
improvised_tools: A 48-hour rule written into the handbook: surface friction to the supervisor within two days of seeing it, no gossip chain first
A mediation script: each side states facts (not motives), the structural cause is named, one concrete agreement is written down
A clean-slate log: agreements recorded, follow-up date set — memory of the conflict expires when the agreement holds
steps: Surface it: the person who saw it tells the supervisor privately within 48 hours — facts, quotes, dates, not interpretations.
Hear both sides separately first: 15 minutes each, facts only. Then name the structural cause out loud ('You own the outcome; she owns her time — that tension is normal.').
Bring them together for 20 minutes: each states what they need (not what the other did wrong), and you write ONE concrete agreement both sign.
Follow up in two weeks: if the agreement held, close it and let the memory expire. If not, reassign roles — not as punishment, as fit.
If the pattern repeats across multiple volunteers with one staffer, the problem is the staffer's management, not the volunteers — address it as supervision, not mediation.
stop_conditions: Stop mediating and escalate to leadership if there is harassment, discrimination, or abuse of power — that is not friction, that is misconduct.
Never take sides publicly before hearing both; the first story is never the whole story, and a premature verdict ends trust.
If either party refuses the agreement process, reassign rather than force — a volunteer who will not engage the process volunteers elsewhere.

title: Build a substitute bench so no role depends on one person
mechanism_check: Every org has a bus factor of one: the pantry manager, the database person, the grant writer. The mechanism is cross-training pairs — every critical role has a trained backup who has DONE the job, not just watched it.
The bench fails when it is theoretical: a backup who trained once two years ago is not a backup. Currency requires quarterly reps.
Building the bench also builds the promotion pipeline: today's backup is tomorrow's lead, and documented cross-training is the resume (nonprofit-024).
improvised_tools: A critical-role map: every role that would halt a program if vacant for a week, with its current backup (or the gap marked red)
Cross-training checklists per role: the 10 tasks the backup must perform supervised before counting as benched
A quarterly drill: the lead takes a real week off (or a simulated one) and the backup runs the role — the only test that counts
steps: Map the critical roles: ask 'what stops if this person is gone a week?' List every role with a yes. Mark current backups or red gaps.
Recruit backups from volunteers and junior staff using the 30-minute training pattern (nonprofit-027), then the supervised checklist.
Run the quarterly drill: lead steps back, backup runs it, lead is reachable only for true emergencies. Debrief what broke.
Document the role as you go: the backup writes the how-to during training — the manual is the byproduct, not a separate project.
Review the map twice a year with leadership: red gaps are a staffing priority, not background noise.
stop_conditions: Stop counting someone as benched if they have not performed the role in 6 months — stale backups fail exactly when needed.
If a lead refuses to train a backup ('job security'), escalate to leadership — hoarded knowledge is an organizational risk, not a personal asset.
Never build the bench by overloading your best people with three backup roles; the bench is distributed or it is decoration.

title: Run a 20-minute after-action review after any event
mechanism_check: Events teach, but only if the lesson is captured before the crew disperses. The mechanism is the hot debrief: within 48 hours, 20 minutes, three questions — what worked, what broke, what changes.
Memory decays fast: a review held two weeks later reconstructs a different event. The 48-hour window is the whole game.
The output is not a report — it is three concrete changes for next time, each with an owner. Unowned lessons are just stories.
improvised_tools: A one-page AAR template: what worked (keep), what broke (fix), three changes with owners and dates
The handoff log and event numbers on hand — the review argues from the record, not from whoever speaks loudest
A blameless rule stated at the start: we review the system, not the people — said out loud, every time
steps: Within 48 hours of the event: gather the captains, 20 minutes, timer on. State the blameless rule.
Round one: what worked — name it specifically so it gets repeated on purpose, not by luck.
Round two: what broke — facts and systems, never names. The log settles disputes about what actually happened.
Decide three changes maximum: each gets an owner and a date. Write them into the template before anyone leaves.
File the AAR where next year's planners will find it, and open the NEXT event's planning with last year's three changes.
stop_conditions: Stop at 20 minutes — a 90-minute post-mortem punishes the crew for showing up and guarantees nobody comes next time.
If the review turns into blame, stop and restate the rule once; if it continues, end the session — a blame session teaches concealment, not improvement.
Never skip the AAR because the event 'went fine' — fine events hide the near-misses that become next year's disasters.
